newsitem.title: USA: Calif. Gov set to sign electricity deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Calif. Gov set to sign electricity deregulation.

text.p: California Governor Pete Wilson plans to sign far-reaching legislation on Monday that would open the state's massive electricity market to competition and slash consumer rates.
Wilson, a Republican, is scheduled to sign the deregulation package at a San Diego ceremony, a spokesman said on Sunday.
The Legislature has already approved the plan, which legislators described as "historic" and a "model" for the nation.

The sweeping legislation will restructure the electricity industry in California, ending the utility monopoly on generation and opening the market to competition so that retail customers can choose power suppliers.

The bill has the support of the large utilities that would be affected most -- Pacific Gas and Electric Co, Enova Corp's San Diego Gas and Electric and Edison International's Southern California Edison.

Supporters of the legislation said deregulation would stimulate the state's economy. Critics contended that the plan was effectively a bailout, negotiated by special interests, for powerful utilities.

Under the legislation, electric utility customers in the state would have a choice of providers as early as January 1998. Municipal utilities would not be required to open their markets, but most were expected to comply voluntarily.
Under the plan control of the transmission lines would be consolidated under a new independent systems operator.

To help the investor-owned utilities better compete as the generation market opens, the utilities would be compensated for certain "stranded" costs, such as nuclear power plants, that would not be economical in a competitive market.

They would be compensated through a system-wide competition transition charge. Under the proposed legislation, from Jan. 1, 1998, to Dec. 31, 2001, the transition charge would come to roughly one to two cents per kilowatt hour.
The charge would help to raise over $28 billion to cover certain stranded costs of the utilities. The utilities already charge customers to cover their stranded costs.
After Dec. 31, 2001, the utilities could extend a smaller transition charge for 10 years or more. While the charge is in place, investor-owned utility rates would be capped.

The legislation would authorise the California Infrastructure Bank to issue up to $10 billion in revenue bonds to enable the utilities to pay off their stranded costs. By issuing the bonds through the state bank, utilities would obtain more favorable interest rates on the debt. State taxpayers would have no obligation or financial exposure.
The proposed bond financings would provide substantial savings to the utilities, and those savings, under the legislation, would be passed on to customers.
The legislation provides for no less than a 10 percent rate reduction beginning in 1998. Residential and small business customers would receive assured rate reductions of at least 20 percent by 2002.
